newsitem.title: USA: FCC struggles to sort out license auction.
newsitem.headline: FCC struggles to sort out license auction.

text.p: Efforts to sort out last year's controversial $10.2 billion wireless phone auction are likely to wind up in court, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and participants predicted on Monday.
Some of the companies that won licenses to develop a new generation of cellular phone service are now laden with debt and have said they may soon be unable to pay the quarterly instalments.
But, representatives of the unsuccessful bidders vowed to take blocking action if the FCC follows proposals to cut the amount of money the winning companies must pay.
"One way or another, I think you're going to see litigation," FCC Wireless Telecommunications Bureau Chief Daniel Phythyon told Reuters.
Phythyon was speaking on the sidelines of a public forum to consider refinancing proposals by some of the winners of the so-called C and F block personal communications services (PCS) licenses.
The winning companies want the FCC to scale the bids back, discount the overall debt, and move to an annual rather than quarterly payment schedule.

Opponents of the restructuring, including some C and F block license holders in good financial standing, said any change in the rules would be unfair and called for re-auctioning of licenses if there was payment default.
"(If the FCC changes the rules,) I'm going to guarantee you litigation," a representative of unsuccessful bidder Antigone Communications told the forum.

Roger Linquist, chief executive officer of license holder General Wireless Inc GWIR.O, shot back by threatening to use the courts to delay any attempt to revoke the licenses. "I can guarantee you substantial delay in the other direction," Linquist said.
Earlier, Phythyon said the FCC was worried that defaulting license holders would be able to use bankruptcy proceedings to hold onto their licenses, further delaying introduction of PCS products.

"One of the unknowns we face is the bankruptcy process and what delays that might bring," Phythyon said, adding that the FCC might consider an amnesty on existing debt and penalties if licenses were handed back without litigation.

Opponents of the restructuring said that license holders should be required to hand back all their licenses if they took advantage of any amnesty, and they should be precluded from bidding for licenses again.
Petitioners for restructuring included top bidder NextWave Communications, which has signed a deal to provide wireless service to MCI Communications Corp.
